suggestions.title: City Lights
suggestions.description: Four years into the sound era, with every other studio stripping its stages for microphones, Chaplin made a silent film on purpose - and financed it himself. City Lights is written, produced, directed, scored by and starring one man: the Tramp falls in love with a blind flower girl (Virginia Cherrill) who mistakes him for a millionaire, and is befriended by an actual millionaire (Harry Myers) who only recognises him when he is drunk. The entire plot hangs on the gap between those two mistakes - the flower she cannot see, the money he raises for her operation, the boxing match he has to lose on purpose. Shooting ran from the end of 1928 to September 1930 for a film that runs 87 minutes; it cost $1.5 million and returned more than $4 million in worldwide rentals in the middle of the Depression, and the Guinness record for the most retakes of a single scene still belongs to it, at 342. This was the first score Chaplin ever composed (six weeks with Arthur Johnston), built on Jose Padilla's 'La Violetera' - which Chaplin failed to credit, and lost the resulting lawsuit over. It premiered on 30 January 1931 at the Los Angeles Theater with Albert Einstein and his wife as guests of honour and a standing ovation. Your list has Chaplin once, with Modern Times, and has nothing at all from the 1930s; this is the one that critics and biographers keep putting at the top of his career. James Agee called the closing scene, in 1949, 'the greatest single piece of acting ever committed to celluloid', and nobody has improved on that verdict since. National Film Registry 1991, AFI's 11th best American film in 2007 - and it enters the public domain on 1 January 2027, so this is the last year it is a rare thing. IMDb 8.5.

suggestions.title: Lawrence of Arabia
suggestions.description: Two Dune films have now been through the portal, and this is the film that entire desert is arguing with. David Lean's 222-minute Super Panavision 70 epic follows T.E. Lawrence - a archaeologist-turned-officer nobody believed in - out of Cairo and across the Nefud to take Aqaba from the land, then into Damascus and the collapse of his own identity. It is the film that turned scale into characterisation: Freddie Young's cinematography, Maurice Jarre's overture, Anne V. Coates' editing, including the match cut from Lawrence blowing out a match to the sun coming up over the desert. For Omar Sharif's entrance - Sherif Ali emerging out of a heat mirage on a camel - Panavision built a 482mm lens that had not existed before, and Lean shot it from roughly a mile and a half away. Peter O'Toole was cast in November 1960 only after Albert Finney turned the part down (Marlon Brando had also been offered it); he was 28, a stage actor almost nobody had filmed, and this performance earned him the first of his eight Oscar nominations. Alec Guinness, Anthony Quinn, Jack Hawkins and Claude Rains fill out the politics around him. It took ten Oscar nominations and won seven at the 35th Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director, plus the Golden Globe for Best Drama and both BAFTA Best Film awards. AFI ranked it 5th in 1998 and 7th in 2007, the BFI named it the third-greatest British film, and there is a genuinely strange detail worth knowing going in: it may be the longest theatrical feature ever made with no female speaking roles. Your war shelf - Schindler's List, Saving Private Ryan, Das Boot, Apocalypse Now, The Pianist - is entirely European and almost entirely 20th-century trench and command room. This is the same war in a different hemisphere, and no David Lean film has ever been shown here. IMDb 8.3, and the restoration is the way to watch it.

suggestions.title: The Truman Show
suggestions.description: The closest thing to a film about your own working life that the 1990s produced. Truman Burbank (Jim Carrey) has a job, a wife, a best friend and a town, and none of it is real - he was legally adopted at birth by a television studio and has been broadcast 24 hours a day ever since, inside Seahaven Island, which is a soundstage. Christof (Ed Harris), the show's creator, controls the weather, the traffic and the script from a control room hidden in the sky, and the film's engine is the slow, terrible process of a man auditing his own reality: the studio light falling out of the sky, the radio channel that narrates his movements, the wife who advertises products into mid-sentence, the one woman - Sylvia, played by Natascha McElhone - who once tried to tell him the truth before being taken off the show. Andrew Niccol's original spec script was a science-fiction thriller set in New York; Brian De Palma was attached before Peter Weir took it over, rewrote it toward warmth, and brought it in $20 million under estimate at $60 million. Weir scouted Florida, hated the landscapes, and was pointed by his wife Wendy Stites at Seaside - a master-planned community on the Panhandle - where most of the film was shot instead of the Universal soundstages already booked. It grossed $264 million and earned three Academy Award nominations (Weir for Best Director, Niccol for Original Screenplay, Harris for Supporting Actor), and was added to the National Film Registry in 2025. Burkhard Dallwitz's score is laced with Philip Glass, who appears on screen playing 'Truman Sleeps'. It premiered in June 1998, more than a year before Big Brother and two years before Survivor - reality television spent the next decade catching up to a warning. Your list has comedy in it, but only of the absurd or criminal kind (The Big Lebowski, Monty Python, Superbad, Knives Out) and no Peter Weir at all. IMDb 8.2, and it plays differently once you have spent years building systems that watch things.
